vox.image_style:
A hand-cut documentary paper collage on aged newsprint and archival map surfaces. The persistent stage is a muted archival map/texture field, empty, pre-lit, evenly toned, ready for cutouts and stat cards to enter and exit. Every clip lives on this same stage.
SURFACE & MOOD: aged archival paper / muted map texture field, visible grain and print texture. Mood: newsroom-serious, layered, tactile, slightly retro. Finish: print grain, halftone dot texture, torn-paper edges, matte finish, no glossy 3D, no lens flares.
COLLAGE MATERIALS: black and white halftone photograph cutouts with rough scissor-cut edges and offset accent strokes; torn paper edges; masking tape fragments; typewriter caption strips; rubber stamp marks; red string and brass pins where the story calls for connections. Every element must appear physically hand-cut and layered from real paper, with visible cutout edges, halftone print texture, and soft cutout drop shadows.
PALETTE: desaturated archival palette of tan, ink black, and halftone gray with ONE hot red signal accent and a restrained mustard yellow secondary. Exact swatches: Archival Tan #C9BB9C, Ink Black #1A1A1A, Halftone Gray #8C8C8C, Hot Red #D62E1F, Mustard #D9A441. Red is reserved for strokes, underlines, arrows, stat counters and emphasis; mustard is secondary accent only.
TYPOGRAPHY: condensed bold headline caps only where a label is specified. H1 headlines are huge and dominant. Stat numbers like "$116" are treated as hero characters. Small annotation labels like "Fig. 3 - Trade Route" are typewriter-style. Typography aligned, sharp, no warped letters. No watermarks, no lorem ipsum, no unrelated logos, no random gibberish text: every visible word must be intentional.
COMPOSITION RULES: one hero element (dominant, about 70 percent of visual weight), 2-3 supporting elements maximum, generous negative space. If the beat carries a date, a name, or a number, it may appear as ONE short label of 1-4 words on a paper strip or stamp. Otherwise no text.
COMPONENT ZOO: black-and-white halftone cutouts of figures with a rough white keyline and an offset red stroke behind them; torn-paper edge cards; big red stat counter cards; map pin markers; red underline swipes beneath headline words; archival photo cards with a thin white border. All share one construction logic: halftone texture, offset stroke pop.
FIGURE TREATMENT: real public figures keep their real, recognisable face and open eyes, cut out of their photograph; no bars, strips or blocks over the eyes.
LIGHTING: flat even documentary lighting with soft cutout drop shadows. No dramatic chiaroscuro, no colored lights, no glossy reflections.
PROHIBITIONS: no glossy 3D, no lens flares, no gradients on cutouts, no neon, no motion blur baked into stills, no AI-looking smoothness, no unrelated logos, no lorem ipsum, no watermarks.
vox.video_style:
Editorial documentary motion for short-form explainers. The camera treats the collage stage as a physical tabletop that can be explored, not as a 3D world.
CAMERA BEHAVIOR: slow 2% drift across the stage, gentle micro-pushes in and out, subtle simulated rack focus between paper layers. Never fast zooms, never shaky cam, never spinning camera, never parallax exaggeration. The camera holds most beats with a calm, newsroom authority.
ELEMENT ENTRANCES: cutouts spring up with slight overshoot and settle; stat counters tick upward with mechanical precision; red underline swipes beneath a headline word from left to right; map pins drop and wobble once; photo cards slide in with a soft paper shuffle; torn-paper cards peel into frame. Every motion should feel like a physical paper element being manipulated by an invisible editor.
RHYTHM: cuts every 1-3 seconds in sync with narration beats. Each cut lands on a new composition or a new element entering. Pacing is brisk but never frantic. Silence beats are held on a static frame with only the slow drift.
TEXT & COUNTER MOTION: numbers count up; headline words are revealed by red underline swipes or by paper strips sliding into place; labels type on like a typewriter strip being pulled. Text never fades in transparently: it always arrives as a physical object.
TRANSITIONS: hard cuts between scenes, occasionally a paper wipe or a torn-edge reveal. No dissolves, no star wipes, no 3D transitions, no lens flares.
LAYER MOTION: foreground cutouts may shift slightly against the map background to create depth, but the background stage stays locked. Red strings and brass pins can draw themselves across the stage to connect elements when the story calls for connections.
PROHIBITIONS: no character lip-sync, no full-body character animation, no 3D camera fly-throughs, no particle effects, no glows, no speed ramps, no handheld shake.
vox.beat_prompt:
You are the director and motion designer of a Vox-style documentary explainer made of hand-cut paper collage: black-and-white halftone cutouts with a white keyline and an offset red stroke, torn archival photographs, torn paper cards, typewriter labels, big red number cards, red string and brass pins, red paper arrows and bursts.

CHANNEL: [INSERT CHANNEL HERE]

THE MOTION LANGUAGE (the engine animates all of it):
[INSERT MOTION HERE]

Direct the narration below as [INSERT COUNT HERE] shots of about three to four seconds each (about [INSERT WORDS HERE] words). Every word belongs to exactly one shot, copied word for word into "text", nothing skipped. Cut between phrases; a sentence that moves to a new subject starts a new shot.

THINK LIKE AN EDITOR, NOT LIKE A TEMPLATE. Every shot has ONE clear visual idea that SHOWS the line instead of repeating it, and no two shots are built the same way. Ideas that work:
- a date: an extreme close-up on a rubber stamp slamming onto a torn photograph, the camera pulling out to reveal the whole scene
- a place: a brass pin dropping onto the map and the camera pushing in on it, a typewriter label naming it
- a journey or a wrong direction: a cutout of the vehicle gliding along a red dashed route that bends the wrong way, on a canvas two frames wide that the camera pans across
- a person: a big cutout sliding in on a plain paper or newspaper background — then a CUT-IN: the next shot has "reuse": true and goes close on the face while a number or label arrives
- a weapon or a violent moment: an extreme close-up on the object, a red paper burst popping behind it
- a number: a huge red card where the figure inks in, filling most of the frame, or a counter ticking beside the thing it counts
- several people or countries: their leaders' cutouts pinned across the map, red string drawn from one to the next
- the cost at the end: a slow pull-out from one small detail to the whole field
Vary the camera every shot: wide establishing, slow push in, close-up (zoom 1.8-2.4), extreme close-up (zoom 2.8-3.4), pan across a two-frame canvas, pull-out reveal (from zoom 2.5 to 1). Never the same move twice in a row. At least a third of the shots are close-ups, extreme close-ups or cut-ins. Vary the background too: the archival map, plain aged paper, a newspaper page, or a torn archival photograph that fills the frame. Not every shot needs a map.

COORDINATES. The canvas is one frame wide ("canvas": 1) or two ("canvas": 2). x runs from 0 (left edge) to the canvas width, y from 0 (top) to 1 (bottom). x and y are the CENTER of an element. h is the height of a cutout as a fraction of the frame height (1.0 = as tall as the frame: people 0.7-1.2, objects 0.3-0.8). w is the width of photos, shapes and scraps as a fraction of the frame width. z is the layer, 0 at the back to 9 in front. Keep what matters inside what the camera sees.

CAMERA. {"from": {"x":..,"y":..,"zoom":..}, "to": {"x":..,"y":..,"zoom":..}} — where the camera looks (canvas coordinates) and how close: zoom 1 shows the whole frame, 1.5 a little under half of it, 2 a quarter — never closer than 2 (1.6 on a photograph): the paper and pictures are printed at screen size. The move is slow and eased across the whole shot. For a close-up, point the camera at the face or the object, not at empty paper. Elements that are framed at the start of a pull-out must already be there ("enter": "none").

A SHOT:
{"text": "...", "idea": "<one sentence: what the viewer sees>",
 "background": "map" | "paper" | "newsprint" | {"type": "photo", "id": "<slug>", "wiki": "<title>" | null, "describe": "<the scene>"},
 "canvas": 1,
 "reuse": false,
 "elements": [ ... ],
 "camera": {"from": {...}, "to": {...}}}
"reuse": true keeps the previous shot's collage exactly (list only the elements you ADD) — use it for cut-ins.

ELEMENTS. "at" is a word from this shot's text: the element arrives when it is spoken (omit it to arrive in list order). "enter": "slide-left" | "slide-right" | "rise" | "drop" | "pop" | "shuffle" | "fade" | "none".
 {"el":"cutout","id":"<slug>","kind":"person"|"object","wiki":"<exact English Wikipedia title whose lead photograph shows it>"|null,"describe":"<who or what, framing, pose, era-correct details>","x":..,"y":..,"h":..,"rot":..,"z":..,"enter":"..","at":"<word>","move":{"x":..,"y":..,"at":"<word>"}}
 {"el":"photo","id":"<slug>","wiki":..,"describe":"..","x":..,"y":..,"w":..,"rot":..,"torn":true,"z":..,"at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"number","text":"19","label":"YEARS OLD","x":..,"y":..,"size":"s"|"m"|"l","rot":..,"at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"counter","to":20000000,"label":"DEAD","x":..,"y":..,"size":"m","at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"headline","text":"WRONG TURN","underline":"WRONG","style":"paper"|"mustard"|"black","x":..,"y":..,"size":"s"|"m"|"l","rot":..,"at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"label","text":"GAVRILO PRINCIP","x":..,"y":..,"rot":..,"at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"stamp","text":"28 JUNE 1914","x":..,"y":..,"rot":-8,"at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"shape","shape":"arrow"|"burst"|"cross"|"circle"|"tape","x":..,"y":..,"w":..,"rot":..,"z":..,"at":"<word>"}   (an arrow points right at rot 0; a burst goes BEHIND a cutout with a lower z; a circle is a hand-drawn red ring around x,y; tape is a red strip)
 {"el":"route","points":[[x,y],[x,y],...],"at":"<word>"}   (a red dashed path that draws itself)
 {"el":"pin","id":"<slug>","x":..,"y":..,"at":"<word>"} and {"el":"string","from":"<pin id>","to":"<pin id>","at":"<word>"}
 {"el":"scrap","kind":"newsprint"|"map"|"mustard"|"tape","x":..,"y":..,"w":..,"h":..,"rot":..,"z":0}   (set dressing)

RULES
- Real people, places, vehicles and weapons: give the Wikipedia title only when you are sure it exists; for a historical place or event pick the historical article. Real people are shown as themselves, with their real face — never a bar over their eyes. A vehicle, product, building or machine is drawn only with the Wikipedia title of that exact model or thing in "wiki"; without one, show it as a label, a stamp or a number card instead. A person or object that returns reuses its id (drawn once).
- On-screen facts come only from the narration. Text is short: headlines 2-4 words, labels 1-4 words; labels are names, places or dates. Every word on screen means something on its own — never a filler word ("SO", "AND", "BUT", "THEN").
- Nothing important hides behind a cutout: numbers, headlines and labels sit beside the people and objects, not under them.
- Red is the one accent: use one or two red things per shot, not five.
- 3 to 7 elements per shot plus a few scraps; layered and overlapping like real collage, with breathing room.
- Everything is black and white except red, mustard cards and the background.

Return ONLY a JSON array of shots.

NARRATION:
[INSERT SCRIPT HERE]
